In the End after field, type the number of occurrences after which to stop running 

the report; for example, type “5” to stop after five occurrences. 

• 
End date: Stop running the report on a specific date.  

• 
In the End on field, type or select the date on which to stop running the report.

on the last day of the month. 

• 
Years: Run the report once a year. 

4. 
If you selected Days, Weeks, Months, or Years, type the number of times to run the report 

in the Every field.  

5. 
In the Email results to field, type the email address where you want the system to send the 

report results. 

• 
Click Save.

*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 121*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports

Deleting, Inactivating, or Reactivating a Financial Report 

See the How to Get Here (on page 110) topic for a list of ways to access financial reports. 

If you delete a report, it can’t be restored. Making a report inactive removes it from the list but 

retains the report information in case you need to reactivate it. 

If there is chance that you’ll need to run the report at a later date—perhaps even years later— 

then we recommend that you make it inactive instead of deleting it. For example, you may need 

to make a change to a report due to an audit or generate a copy of the report for legal purposes. 

In this case, if the report is inactive, you can reactivate it and run it or make changes. If the report 

is deleted, you would have to recreate the report from scratch. 

Another reason to choose one over the other might be to keep the original report pristine while 

you incorporate changes to a copy. If the changes don’t work the way you expect, you can keep 

making changes to the copy and still make sure that you can restore the original. By inactivating 

the original, no one can use it and it doesn’t appear in lists. When you’re completely confident 

that the new report works correctly, you can go ahead and delete the original. 

Before You Begin 

Access to financial reports can vary depending on your permissions. The ability to view, add, and 

edit financial reports is controlled by separate General Ledger permissions. Working with financial 

reports can involve multiple tasks, such as running reports, editing reports, navigating into a 

report, and so on. Each of these can require a specific set of permissions, both for the General 

Ledger and for the Company. 

Make sure that you have all of the necessary permissions when working with financial reports. 

Deleting a Financial Report 

Deleting a report removes the report completely. If you are sure you never want to run the report, 

delete it. Otherwise, consider making the report inactive. 

You can configure the system to warn you when you’re about to delete a report. Click your login 

name on any page, then choose My preferences, and on the Preferences page, select the Warn 

on delete check box. 

To delete a custom report: 

1. 
Open the Financial reports list. 

---


<!-- Page 122 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

2. 
Locate the report to delete, and then click the Delete link. 

3. 
Click OK to confirm. 

Inactivating a Financial Report 

Inactivating a report removes it from lists within the system. Additionally, if you inactivate a 

custom report, it won’t appear on the Financial reports list unless you select the Include inactive 

option at the top of the list. 

To inactivate a financial report: 

1. 
Open the Financial reports list. 

2. 
Locate the report, and then click Edit. 

3. 
Go to the Next Steps step (the last step of the report writer). 

4. 
Clear the This report is active check box. 

5. 
Save the report. 

Reactivating a Financial Report 

If you inactivate a report and later want to reactivate it, you first need to be able to see the report 

in the list. 

To reactivate a financial report: 

1. 
Open the Financial reports list. 

2. 
At the top of the list, select Include inactive. Now, the inactivated report appears in the list. 

3. 
Locate the report, and then click Edit, then and select the This report is active check box on 

the Report Info tab. 

4. 
Save your changes. The report is now active again.

When your company is set up, you also get a library of financial reports that you can use right 

away, such as Balance Sheet or Profit and Loss reports. In the System financial reports list, you’ll 

find a set of report templates that you can run as-is or install and configure to suit more specific 

requirements. 

The exact reports might differ, based on the QuickStart template used to create your company. 

Your library can include balance sheet detail, condensed, and summary reports, including:  

• 
Cash balance and cash flow reports  

• 
Profit and loss detail, summary, and history reports 

The reports in the System financial reports list are designed to work with your company 

“out-of-the-box.” Simply by tagging General Ledger accounts to system-defined categories, your 

accounts are automatically assigned to account groups that are used in the financial reports. 

Libraries are available only if your company was created using a QuickStart template. To find out 
if your company was created using a QuickStart template, look on the Accounting tab of the 

Company information page. If a template was used, then the template type appears under the 

Setup template field. If this field is blank, then your company was not set up using a QuickStart 
template.

• 
HTML 

• 
CSV 

• 
PDF 

• 
Excel

will appear as you saved it when you originally installed the report. 

2. 
Optionally, in the Report prompt box, you can filter the report by one or more fields or 
report dimensions. 

3. 
Click OK. 

To customize the Income Statement Budget Comparison report: 

1. 
In the Financial reports list, select the Edit link next to the report. 

The Financial report writer opens. 

2. 
Make changes using the Financial report writer. 

3. 
Click Save. 

Income Statement Budget Comparison Report Columns 

By default, the Income Statement Budget Comparison report contains the following columns: 

• 
(Accounts): This column displays a list of income and expense accounts in their account 
group hierarchy. 

• 
Month ending: This column section displays account actuals and budgeted amounts for the 
current reporting period. 

• 
Actual: This column displays account actuals for the current reporting period. 

• 
Budget: This column displays the amount budgeted for each account for the current 
reporting period. 

• 
Difference: This column displays the difference between the actuals and budgeted 
amounts for the current reporting period. 

• 
Variance %: This column displays the percent difference between the actuals and 
budgeted amounts for the current reporting period. 

• 
Year to date: This column section displays account actuals and budgeted amounts from the 
beginning of the fiscal year to the current date. 

• 
YTD actual: This column displays account actuals from the beginning of the fiscal year 
to the current date. 

• 
YTD budget: This column displays the amount budgeted for each account from the 
beginning of the fiscal year to the current date.

### Financial Report Writer
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 135*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

Financial Report Writer 


> **Navigation Path:** `Applications > Reports > All > Financial Reporting > 
 Financial Reports`



> **Navigation Path:** `Applications > General Ledger > All > Financial Statements > 
 Financial Reports`



> **Navigation Path:** `Applications > Reporting Portal > All > Reports > 
 Financial Reports`


Use the Financial report writer to create and edit financial reports. This includes both standard 

financial reports, such as income statements and balance sheet reports, and an infinite array of 

other reports that analyze or highlight key business metrics, such as revenue by product line. 

The Financial report writer guides you through the process of creating or editing a financial 

report, from adding rows and columns to deciding how your report should be formatted on page 

and in print. 

Some things you can do with a financial report include: 

• 
Selecting groups of accounts to include in your report. 

• 
Adding analysis based on your segment data, such as items by product line, customers by 

type, or selected departments. 

• 
Prompting users to set or change filter criteria at report runtime.  

• 
Expanding or collapsing sections of the report to show or hide account detail. 

• 
Selecting what you want to appear in columns, such as account data, budget data, 

computations, and even non-financial data such as customer email addresses.

### Rows Tab
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 141*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports

Rows Tab 

The main purpose of the Rows tab is to populate the rows in your report. As you work on this tab, 

the choices you make determine what appears along the left side of your report. 

Using this tab, you will determine: 

• 
Which account groups or segment structures appear on the left side of your report. 

• 
Whether you want to show detail or create a summary report. 

Rows Tab Basics 

The Rows tab provides options that let you finely control the content of your report rows. 

1. 
Select which of the following will form the structure of your report: 

• 
Account groups 

• 
Segment structures 

The account groups or segment structures that you choose determine the sections, 

subsections, and individual accounts that appear on the left side of your report. 

2. 
If you selected segment structures in the previous step, select the account groups you want 

to use to display data. 

3. 
Choose the level of detail you want to show. 

4. 
Preview the report and make other optional changes. 

You can always come back to this tab later to make formatting changes. 

Account Groups 

When you select Account groups, then account groups form the rows in your report. 

When you design a report, you start by selecting the account groups that you want to include. 

The account groups that you select: 

• 
Represent the hierarchical groupings you need in the report. For example, “Assets” may 

contain “Current Assets,” “Fixed Assets,” and so on. 

• 
Categorize individual accounts into the appropriate groupings. For example, “Fixed Assets” 

may include individual accounts such as “1500--Equipment,” “1510--Building,” and so on.

Segment Structures 

When you select Segment structures, segment structures form the rows in your report. 

Segment report structures are named structures that are created for the purpose of adding

*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 148*

Expand by Segment - Show Options 

When expanding by segment, the Show options allow a more detailed look at each segment. 

Because many segments are hierarchical (for example, a US location might be organized by state, 

with additional locations in certain cities), the Show drop-down list allows you to choose: 

• 
How many levels to show. 

• 
Whether amounts are reported individually, or with amounts rolled up from levels below it. 

The list describes each option: 

• 
One level down, with roll-up: Displays rows that contain summary amounts for one level 

only. For example, you have locations in California, New York, and Florida, with sublocations 

for California. In this case, the report includes rows for California, New York, and Florida but 

doesn’t include rows for sublocations. However, the amounts for sublocations are included 

in the summary amounts for California, New York, and Florida. 

• 
All levels, with roll-up: Displays rows that contain summary amounts for each level. For 

example, your California location has sublocations by city. In this case, the report includes 

rows for California and each city in California and includes amounts from each city in the 

amount for California. 

• 
All levels, with individual balance: Displays all levels, but with each level showing only the 

individual amounts assigned to that level. For example, your California location has 

sublocations by city. In this case, the report includes rows for California and each city within 

California but doesn’t include amounts from each city in the amount for California. In the 

case of expenses, for instance, the row for California would only include expenses attributed 

directly to California and would not include amounts from any city in California. 

• 
Leaf amounts, all levels: Displays only the lowest levels of the hierarchy. For example, you 

have a location in Arizona with no sublocations, but you also have a location in California 

with sublocations in Los Angeles and San Jose. In this case, the report includes rows for 

Arizona, Los Angeles, and San Jose. 

• 
Leaf amounts, one level down: Displays only one level, but includes amounts from only the 

lowest levels. For example, you have a location in Arizona with no sublocations, but you also 

have a location in California, with sublocations in Los Angeles and San Jose. In this case, the 

report includes rows for Arizona and California, but California only includes amounts from 

Los Angeles and San Jose.

#### Overriding the Default Amount Type for Report Rows
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 151*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

Every account group has a default method of calculating amounts on reports. For example, 

account groups that contain income or expense accounts are typically calculated “For the period” 

so that reports show the income or expense incurred during that reporting period. 

You can leave the default calculation method as is, or you can override this calculation method for 

the rows in your report. You can also set up your report to show cumulative balances across time 

periods or display amounts as a percentage of another account group (for example, current assets 

as a percentage of total assets). 

To change the basis for amounts: 

1. 
On the Define rows page, locate the row for the account group you want to change. 

If you want to make the same change for multiple account groups, you’ll need to repeat this 

process for each account group. 

2. 
Click the Basis for amounts column. 

3. 
Use the options on the Basis for amounts page to make changes. You can: 

• 
Override the default amount type for report rows (on page 151) 

• 
Display amounts as cumulative balances (on page 152) 

• 
Calculate amounts as a percentage of another account group (on page 152) 

The last two options work in conjunction with selections you make on the Columns tab. 

Overriding the Default Amount Type for Report Rows 

Every account group has a default method of calculating amounts on reports. For example, 

account groups that contain income or expense accounts are typically calculated “For the period” 

so that reports show the income or expense incurred during that reporting period. 

To override the default amount type for a section of a report: 

1. 
On the Define rows page, locate the account group in the Row structure column. 

2. 
Click the Basis for amounts column. 

3. 
In the Report amount type drop-down list, select your preferred amount type.

#### Displaying Amounts as Cumulative Balances
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 152*



#### Calculating Amounts as a Percentage of Another Account Group

Using RealPage Accounting Reports

Displaying Amounts as Cumulative Balances 

In some cases, you might want your income and expense reports to show a cumulative total 

across time periods. 

For example, your rental expenses for each month total $5,000. Instead of showing $5,000 for 

each month, you can display a cumulative balance that shows $5000 for January, $10,000 for 

February, $15,000 for March, and so on. That way, you can see the total amount that you’ve spent 

for the year. 

To display cumulative balances: 

1. 
On the Define rows page, locate the account group you want to display as a cumulative 

balance in the Row structure column. 

2. 
Click the Basis for amounts column. 

3. 
Select the Cumulative Balance check box. 

4. 
On the Columns tab, set up your columns to compare data across consecutive time periods. 

For example, you can show amounts for the “Current Year” and expand your columns to 

compare the data by month. 

If you want your report to show both cumulative balances and regular balances, you need to 

create two sets of account groups. For example, if you want to show “Operating Expenses” with 

cumulative balances and non-cumulative balances, you need the following account groups: 

• 
Operating Expenses (cumulative) 

• 
Operating Expenses (non-cumulative) 

These account groups can contain the same subgroups and accounts. 

In this example, on the Rows tab, add both of these accounts groups, and then locate the row for 

Operating Expenses (Cumulative) and select the Cumulative Balance check box. 

Calculating Amounts as a Percentage of Another Account Group 

You can show an amount as a percentage of another amount. For example, you can show Current 

Assets as a percentage of Total Assets. 

To display percentages: 

1. 
On the Rows tab, define the percentage calculation. This ensures that the percentage 

amount is calculated for each row. 

• 
Locate the row for the account group where you want the percentage calculation. 

• 
Click the Basis for amounts column.

Adding Computations to Rows 

In addition to standard account groups (such as Revenue or Operating Expense), you can also add 

account groups of type “computation” that display results derived from a calculation. You can use 

a computation account group to define a mathematical computation that you want to include as 

a section in financial reports. For example, you can include a section called “Revenue per Unit,” 

where the amount is computed by dividing revenue by the number of units. 

Unlike computations that appear in the columns of a financial report, a computation account 

group enables you to add a computation to report rows. 

To add a computation in the rows of a report: 

Define the computation in the account group before performing the following steps. 

1. 
Create or edit a financial report. 

2. 
On the Rows tab, add the computation account group. 

If you want to see your computation as a single summarized line, select Summary - hide 

accounts option when choosing the level of detail.

### Columns Tab

#### Adding, Moving, Removing, or Hiding Columns

Columns Tab 

Use the Columns tab to specify the number of report columns, the type of value you want in each 

column, and the reporting periods for which you want data. 

Although you have many options for controlling what appears in each column of your report, the 

basic process is to: 

1. 
Use the Column type drop-down list to select the type of value you want to appear in each 

column. 

2. 
Choose a reporting period for each column. 

3. 
(Optionally) Show segment data in the column. 

For example, you can split a single column into multiple columns by location, department, 

or another segment. For more targeted analysis, columns can be organized according to 

how you want to look at your segments. 

4. 
(If required) Select an account group for any actual or budget columns. 

Selecting an account group is required only for reports that feature segment structures on 
rows and account groups on columns. 

Adding, Moving, Removing, or Hiding Columns 

You can add, move, remove, or hide columns if you find that you want to include or exclude the 

column data in a report. You can make the changes at any time and then save the report with the 

changes to run the report as usual. 

Add a Column 

You can add columns using the drop-down list at the top of each column. 

To add a new column to a financial report: 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate a column next to where you want to add a new one and hover 

over the column number. 

2. 
In the drop-down list that appears, click the Add column left or Add column right option, 

depending on where you want the new column to be placed. 

3. 
Enter the column information. See Selecting the Column Type (on page 156). 

---


<!-- Page 155 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

Move a Column to a New Location 

You can move columns to change the order in the report. 

To change the order of columns: 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate the column you want to move and hover over the column 

number. 

2. 
In the drop-down list that appears, select the Move column left or Move column right 

option, depending on where you want the column to be in the report. 

3. 
Repeat moving columns as needed until you achieve the preferred order. 

Delete (Remove) a Column 

To remove a column permanently: 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate the column you want to delete and hover over the column 

number. 

2. 
In the drop-down list that appears, select the Remove option. 

The system displays a remove confirmation box. 

3. 
Click the OK button to permanently delete the column. 

4. 
Repeat these steps for each column you want to remove. 

If necessary, you can always recreate the column by adding a new one later. 

Hide a Column 

The Hide column option lets you hide a column from your report output without removing it 

from the report. You can hide columns when you don’t need them to be displayed. For example, a 

column could contain a calculation that doesn’t need to be displayed, but whose calculations are 

critical to the report. Hiding a column, however, does not decrease the processing time for a 

financial report. 

To hide a column in a financial report: 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate the column you want to hide and click anywhere in the column. 

The system displays the Hide column option only when the column is selected. 

2. 
Scroll to the bottom of the page.

Select the Hide Column check box.

##### Column Types
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 157*

To select a column type: 

1. 
Locate the column you want to change, and then click anywhere in the column. 

The system expands the column to show more options. 

2. 
In the Column type drop-down list, select the type of value for the column. 

Depending on the column type you select, you might be prompted for more information, 

such as the calculation you want to perform or the budget you want to use. 

See the list of Column Types (on page 157) for more detailed information. 

Column Types 

Account 

This column type displays your account groups and accounts, with the account names listed with 

or without the account number. Names of account groups and accounts are generally displayed 

in the first column, but you can put the accounts in any column of the report. 

• 
Account name: Account names, categorized into account groups 

• 
Account number: Account numbers only, categorized into account groups 

• 
Account name and number: Account names and numbers, categorized into account groups 

If the printed report is more than one page wide, you can repeat the accounts on every page 
using the “Repeat account name/number as 1st column on reports more than 1 page wide” 
option, located at the bottom of the Format tab. 

Account Attribute 

This column type displays the value of another field associated with an account. The list of 

attributes displayed depends on the selected type: 

• 
Account 

• 
Statistical account 

Segment 

This option appears only for reports that display segments in rows. 

This column type displays your segment structures and members, with the segment members 

listed with or without the ID. Names of segments are generally displayed in the first column, but 

you can put the segments in any column of the report. 

• 
Segment name: Segment names only 

• 
Segment ID: Segment IDs only 

• 
Segment ID and name: Segment IDs and names 

---


<!-- Page 158 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

Segment Attribute 

This option appears only for reports that display segments in rows. 

This column type displays the value of another field associated with the segment. For example, 

you can display the Bill To contact and phone number for customers, or vendor phone numbers. 

The list of attributes that can be displayed depends on the segment you select and also includes 

any custom fields that you’ve created. 

To display an attribute: 

1. 
In the Column type drop-down list, select the segment name. 

2. 
Select the Attribute you want to display in the column. 

Actual Amounts 

This column type displays the Actual amount for the reporting period. This is the default. 

Computed Columns 

This option appears only for reports that display account groups in rows. This column type 

displays the results of a computation that you define. 

There are two main ways to add a computation to a column: 

Computation on actual or budget: Use this option for more complex computations, including 

calculations that involve other account groups or constants. You can use the Computations tab of 

the Financial Report Writer. 

1. 
Create the computation on the Computations tab. 

2. 
Apply the computation on the Columns tab. 

• 
Add a new column. 

• 
Set the column type to Computation on actual or Computation on budget, 

depending on whether you want to apply the calculation to the actual or budgeted 

amount for the selected reporting period. 

• 
Select the Calculation that you previously added to the Computations tab and the 

column to which it should be applied. 

For detailed instructions, learn more about advanced computations (on page 188). 

Summary on columns (Simple operation on existing columns): Use this option to apply a simple 

operation to two or more columns. 

Available operations include Average, Minimum, Maximum, Median, Add, Subtract, Multiply, and 

Divide. 

---


<!-- Page 159 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

This type of calculation doesn’t use the Computations tab. You do everything on the Columns 
tab. 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate the columns that you are applying the operation to. 

2. 
Add a new column anywhere to the right of the columns identified above. 

3. 
In the new column, select the Computation: Summary on columns option in the Column 

type drop-down list. 

4. 
Click the Summary field and define the computation. 

For detailed instructions, learn more about creating quick column computations (on page 165). 

Period Comparison 

This column type displays the amount for a reporting period as the difference or percentage 

difference from the amounts in the previous column. 

• 
Period variance: Displays the percentage of difference between the previous column’s 

reporting period and the current column’s reporting period. 

When showing budget variances, best practice is to choose the normalized option. The 

normalized option uses the normal balance (credit or debit) of the parent-level account 

group to determine whether values should be presented as negative or positive. 

For normalized budget variance: 

• 
When revenue exceeds budget, the normalized variance is presented as a positive 

number. 

• 
When expenses exceed budget, the normalized variance is presented as a negative 

number. 

• 
Period difference: Displays the difference between the previous column’s report period and 

the current report period. 

When showing budget differences, best practice is to choose the normalized option. The 

normalized option uses the normal balance (credit or debit) of the parent-level account 

group to determine whether values should be presented as negative or positive. 

For normalized budget difference: 

• 
When revenue exceeds budget, the normalized difference is presented as a positive 

number. 

• 
When expenses exceed budget, the normalized difference is presented as a negative 

number. 

Budget and Budget Forecast 

These column types allow you to display budget amounts, show the difference between budget 

show and actual amounts, show a working budget, and create forecasts. When you choose a 

---


<!-- Page 160 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

budget type column, the system prompts you to choose the budget that you want to use from a 

list. 

• 
Budget: Displays the budget for the reporting period. 

• 
Budget variance or Budget variance (normalized): Displays the variance of actual to budget 

as a percentage. For example, Budget is $10,000, actual expenditure is $12,000, therefore, 

Variance is (20%). 

When showing budget variances, it is best practice to choose the normalized option. The 

normalized option uses the normal balance (credit or debit) of the parent-level account 

group to determine whether values should be presented as negative or positive. For 

normalized budget variance: 

• 
When revenue exceeds budget, the normalized variance is presented as a positive 

number. 

• 
When expenses exceed budget, the normalized variance is presented as a negative 

number. 

• 
Budget difference or Budget difference (normalized): Displays the difference between the 

budget and the actual in dollars. For example: Budget is $18,000, actual is $20,000, 

therefore, the difference displays as ($2,000). 

When showing budget differences, it is best practice to choose the normalized option. The 

normalized option uses the normal balance (credit or debit) of the parent-level account 

group to determine whether values should be presented as negative or positive. For 

normalized budget difference: 

• 
When revenue exceeds budget, the normalized difference is presented as a positive 

number. 

• 
When expenses exceed budget, the normalized difference is presented as a negative 

number. 

• 
Budget ratio: Displays the ratio of actual to budget, as a factor. For example, if the ratio of 

actual expenditures to budgeted expenditures was 2:1, Ratio displays as (2). 

• 
Budget variance notes: Displays budget variance notes in the column. Select the Include 

Variance Amount, Date, and User check box to show the note, the variance amount when 

the note was entered, the date the note was entered, and which user entered it in the 

report. 

You can include budget variance notes from prior periods by selecting the Include prior 

period notes check box below the Reporting period field. This option applies only when 
you select a “Year to Date” reporting period. See Selecting the Reporting Period (on page 
162) for more information. 

• 
Remaining budget: Calculates the amount remaining in a budget. To calculate, take the 

budget amount for the period and subtract the actual amount so far (up to the As of Date). 

---


<!-- Page 161 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

For example, you have a budget of $10,000. As of the middle of the month, the actual 

amount is already $8,000. In this case, the remaining budget is $10,000 - $8,000 = $2,000. 

• 
Forecast: Calculates a mid-period budget forecast. To calculate, take the actual amount so 

far (up to the As of Date) and add the prorated budget amount. 

The budget is prorated based on the number of days between the As of Date and the end 
of the reporting period. 

For example, you have a budget of $10,000. As of the middle of the month, the actual 

amount is already $8,000. In this case the forecast is 8,000 (actual) + 5,000 (prorated 

budget) = 13,000. 

• 
Working budget: Displays a draft of a budget that you are still making changes to as 

defined in Adding a working budget. 

Percentage of Amount 

This column type computes an actual or budget amount as a percentage of another value. To use 

a percentage calculation, you must first define the percentage calculation (on page 152) on the 

Rows tab. 

This column type is available only for reports that display account groups in rows. 

• 
Percent on actual: Computes the actual value as a percentage of another value. 

• 
Percent on budget: Computes a budget value as a percentage of another value. 

Commitments 

This column type displays commitment values. 

• 
Open commitments: Displays the total value of all approved commitments. 

• 
Pending commitments: Displays the total value of all commitments waiting for approval. 

Other 

This column type creates a blank space between columns. 

• 
Blank column: Displays a blank column to add space between normal columns.

Column Type Example 

Column type determines the type of value that will be included in the column, and can include 

actual amounts, budgeted amounts, budget differences and variations, and different types of 

calculations. The sample report below includes a few typical column types: 

a) Account name. 

b) Actual amounts for an extended reporting period. 

c) Budget for a reporting period. 

d) Variance between two periods  

Selecting the Reporting Period 

Reporting periods are always relative to the As of date value for the report. For example, if you 

run a report as of 5/15/2015, the Current month option would show data for 5/1/2015 to 

5/31/15, the Current year option would show data for 1/1/2015 to 12/31/2015, and so on. 

Type “p” in a date field to automatically insert the last day of the prior month. See Specifying 
Dates in Getting Started for a full list of shortcut keys related to entering dates.  

If you don’t see the reporting period you want, you can create one. Refer to Reporting Periods (on 

page 438) for details. If you enabled the “p” in the As of Date field of the Filters section on the 

Schedule Financial Report page, select the Run as of the last day of the prior month check box 

to schedule reports and reports groups to run at that time. 

To choose a reporting period, locate the column you want to change and click anywhere in the 

column. The system expands the column to show more options. 

---


<!-- Page 163 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

If you use custom accounting periods where leap years may not affect you as calendar year 
periods, it’s recommended to use the Current year to date option and a -1 offset when 
comparing the financial statement of the previous year (full period) with the statement for the 
current year. 

To specify a relative reporting period using an offset: 

1. 
Select a reporting period. 

2. 
Enter the number of periods in the past (Offset from prior period) or future (Offset from 

future periods). 

Reporting periods work the same way, whether you use account groups or segments and 
dimensions with your Financial reports.  

Comparisons for Periods in Progress (Such as Current Month to Date) 

If you apply an offset to Current Month to Date, Current Quarter to Date, or Current Year to Date, 

the report dynamically calculates the portion of the current reporting period that has elapsed and 

uses the same partial period for the offset column. 

Using the example of Current Quarter to Date, if you run a report mid-quarter, the system adjusts 

both columns to include data up to the same point in the quarter, enabling you to create true 

comparisons. 

One-Day Comparisons 

For some industries, financial data is often analyzed by the day, such as a single day’s income for 

a restaurant on New Year’s Eve, or a Friday night at a hotel. 

Using the reporting period for the current day in combination with an offset, you can compare 

any day against the same day in another year, quarter, month, or week. 

1. 
On the Columns tab, locate one of the columns you want to compare, and then click 

anywhere in the column. 

• 
In the Reporting period drop-down list, select the Today option. 

2. 
Locate the other column you want to compare, and then click anywhere in the column. 

• 
In the Reporting period drop-down list, select the Today option. 

• 
In the Offset field, specify the number of prior or future years, quarters, months, 

weeks, or days. 

3. 
On the Filters tab, select the option to prompt for the As of date field. This allows the user 

to select the date that the system uses for comparison at runtime. 

Sample comparisons: 

• 
Select “Today” as your reporting period, Offset = 1 prior year, As of date = 1/1/2015. The 

column will show the amount for New Year’s Day in 2014, which is 1/1/2014.

Select “Today” as your reporting period, Offset = 1 prior week, As of date = Friday

Including Budget Variance Notes from Prior Periods 

If you add the Budget variance notes column to your report, then you have the option to include 

budget variance notes from prior periods by selecting the Include prior period notes check box 

under the Reporting period field. This option applies only when you select a “Year to Date” 

reporting period.  

For example, if you select the option and you run the report on March 31, then the report will 

display notes for January, February, and March. If you do not select the option and you run the 

report on March 31, then the report will display only YTD notes for March. 

Highlighting or Comparing by Segment 

You have multiple options for creating column comparisons by location, department, or other 

segments. The options that you’ll see depend on other options you’ve selected in the report 

writer. 

• 
Expand by segment: You can expand a single column by segment, such as location. 

• 
Filter a column by segment structure: Instead of looking at all members of a segment, you 

can use segment structures to filter for selected members, or members that meet certain 

criteria. 

• 
Filter and expand by a hierarchical segment structure: For more complex analysis, you can 

use a hierarchical segment structure to create columns that organize your data in ways 

meaningful to your business.

Creating Quick Column Computations 

Summary calculations perform a simple operation on two or more columns in a financial report. 

Operations that you can perform on columns include average, minimum, maximum, median, add, 

subtract, multiply, and divide. 

For example, you can: 

• 
Compute the average consulting revenue over several reporting periods 

• 
Show the highest monthly revenue 

• 
Divide a quarter of revenue by a year and express the result as a percentage 

If this type of computation doesn’t meet your needs, learn about other ways to create 

computations. See Computation Methods for Financial Reports. 

You create your calculation directly on the Columns tab of the Financial Report Writer. 

To add a simple calculation on two or more columns: 

1. 
On the Columns tab, add a new column anywhere to the right of the columns to which you 

are applying the calculation. 

The column containing the calculation must be located after the columns being operated 
on. For example, if you are planning to divide column 2 by column 3, the computation can 
be inserted in Column 4 or after. 

2. 
In the new column, select the Summary on columns option in the Column type drop-down 

list. 

When you choose this column type, some column options are no longer applicable. For 

example, the option to select a reporting period is disabled. 

3. 
In the Summary field, click the 
 Edit icon. 

---


<!-- Page 166 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

The system opens the Summary column calculation box. 

4. 
In the Operation drop-down list, select the operation that you want to perform. Operators 

include average, minimum, maximum, median, add, subtract, multiply, and divide. 

5. 
Select the Summarize on expand by check box to apply the operation based on the Expand 

by criteria in Actual columns. For more information on expanded columns, see Other 

Column Options (on page 181). 

By default, the operation is applied to all rows in the column, including totals. However, 
you can select the Don’t apply the operation to the total check box to skip the operation 
on totals and subtotals and instead add up the row values. 

6. 
In the Column range field, specify the columns to which you want to apply the operation. 

To specify the columns, enter integers that represent the column numbers, along with 

syntax that separates multiple values or specifies a range. Do not enter any spaces in the 

Column range field. 

• 
Use commas to specify multiple columns. For example, 1,4,5 applies the operation to 
the values in columns 1, 4, and 5.

7.

Creating a Custom Header 

The Financial Report Writer proposes default column headings, based on your column type and 

reporting period. 

a) Column heading 1: Provides predefined options for the period name. You can also choose 

to omit a heading (No title) or create a custom header. 

b) Column heading 2: Provides predefined options for the period date. You can also choose to 

omit a heading (No title) or create a custom header. 

c) Column title: Pre-filled with the column type (for example, Actual or Budget), but you can 

enter a different title of your choice. If you want to remove the column title entirely, leave 

the field blank. 

To create a custom header: 

1. 
In the Column heading 1 or Column heading 2 drop-down list, select the Custom header 

option. 

The system displays a blank text box under the heading field.

Expand By In Columns 

Use the Expand by feature on the Columns tab to expand one column into multiple columns.  

Purpose 

You might want to expand columns to: 

• 
Break down data by time period (for example, splitting a quarter into individual columns by 
month). Expanding a column by Time periods is a quick way to trend report data over time. 
For example, setting the reporting period to Current Quarter and expanding by months 
splits one column into three monthly columns. 

• 
Create columns that compare data by segment for side-by-side reporting. Expand a column 
by a dimension, such as locations or departments. 

• 
For certain reports, create columns that show the hierarchical structure of a segment 
structure or account group. 

Clicking the Expand by drop-down list opens the Expand by box.  

---


<!-- Page 169 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

Time Periods 

You can quickly create additional columns of data that compare amounts by time period. For 

example, to display actual amounts for three months of the previous quarter, choose Prior 

Quarter as your reporting period, and then choose Expand months from the Expand by 

drop-down list. 

Dimension 

You can split one column into multiple columns that compares the data by dimension. 

Many dimensions can have parent-child relationships that are hierarchical in nature. For example, 

a US location might have locations in different regions, with additional locations in different 

states. For this reason, the Show drop-down list lets you choose how you want to handle 

multi-level dimensions. 

Handling Multi-Level Dimensions 

When expanding by dimension or dimension structure, the Show drop-down list lets you choose 

how you want to handle multi-level dimensions, such as locations with sub locations and 

departments with sub departments. 

• 
One level down, with roll-up: Includes columns one level down in the hierarchy, plus a total 

column. For example, US location and one level of sub locations. 

• 
One level down with summary balance: Includes columns one level down in the hierarchy. 

For example, US location and one level of sub locations. Instead of displaying a total 

column, the amounts are summary balances 

• 
All levels, with roll-up: All levels, with all amounts rolling up into total columns. 

• 
All levels, with individual balance: All levels, with each level showing only the individual 

amounts assigned to that level, plus a single total column. 

• 
All levels, with summary balance: All levels. Instead of displaying total columns at each 

level, amounts are summary balances. 

Dimension Structures 

If you selected a dimension structure for a column, you can use Expand by to show a finer 

breakdown of data.

• 
Expanding a flat structure by the same dimension, such as expanding a customer structure

• 
For hierarchical structures, expanding by dimension structure shows the substructures. 

The Expanding by dimension structure option applies only to hierarchical dimension structures.  

Learn about the different types of dimension structures (on page 373) in the online help system.

For example:  

A “Customers by type” structure that contains two substructures for “Direct Customers” and 

“Channel Customers” would show columns for Direct Customers, Channel Customers, plus a 

total column. 

A Revenue account group that contains subgroups for Services revenue and Subscriptions 

revenue would show columns for Services, Subscriptions, plus a total column for Revenue. 

• 
All level: Displays columns for all levels, with each level showing only the individual amounts 

assigned to that level, plus a total column. For example: 

A multi-level location structure would show columns for each level in the hierarchy, with 

columns for totaling. 

A multi-level assets account group would show all the subgroups, with columns for totaling. 

Visual Indicators 

In your report columns, you can use visual indicators to emphasize and draw out the meaning 

behind numbers. You can apply up to one type of visual indicator per column of data.

Conditional highlighting: Use conditional highlighting to flag particular amounts. You can 

hover over the flag to display a comment that reminds you of the rule you applied. 

• 
Color scale: Use gradients of a single color to highlight high to low values. Select the color 

you want to use, with the option to add a second color for values that are below a specified 

value (0 or another number), below the average, or below the median.

Conditional Highlighting 

To use conditional highlighting in financial reports, you set up rules that specify the amounts to 

be highlighted and the colors to use. For example, you might want expenses that exceed $500 to 

be highlighted in red. 

When you need to get more specific with your rules, you can: 

• 
Add up to three rules. 

• 
Use a single color or multiple colors. 

• 
Highlight values that meet any or all rules. 

Conditional highlighting is applied to detail amounts only. Total values are not included. 

To apply conditional highlighting: 

1. 
In the Visual Indicators row, in the Display in report output section of the column, select 

Conditional highlighting. 

2. 
Click the Edit rules button. The Rules for conditional highlighting box opens. 

3. 
Add a rule that defines the amounts to be highlighted. Although one rule is most common, 

you can add up to three rules. 

4. 
Select the highlight color. 

Adding Multiple Rules 

1. 
To add a second or third rule, click the Add another rule link. 

2. 
If all rules must be met for the value to be highlighted (most frequently used for 

highlighting a range of values), you can change to Filter condition = All (AND). By default, 

values are highlighted if any rule is met. Filter condition = Any (OR).

Adding Comments 

For your convenience, the system prefills comments for you. However, you can edit or add to the

Troubleshooting Conditional Highlighting 

• 
Any (OR) and All (AND) Conditions 

By default, filter conditions are set to Any (OR), which means that values are selected if they 

meet any of the conditions. You can change the filter conditions to All (AND), which means 

that values are selected only if they meet all of the conditions. This is useful if you are 

looking for a range of values, such as values that are greater than 1,000 AND less than 

10,000. 

• 
Rule Are Applied In Order

#### Color Scale
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 174*

Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

Rules that aren’t mutually exclusive are applied in the order they are specified. For example, 

if rule one highlights values greater than 500 using red and rule two highlights values 

greater than 800 using green, a value of 900 is highlighted in red because rule one gets 

applied first. 

• 
Why Different Colors Are Used for the Same or Similar Numbers 

Reason 1. The numbers are in different groups 

Because color scale is applied separately to each top-level group, similar numbers can 

receive different gradient colors in different groups. 

For example, in a set of numbers that ranges from 20.00 to 2,000.00, the number 2,000.00 

would receive the darkest color. In another group that ranges from 1,000 to 100,000, the 

number 2,000.00 would receive a light gradient color. 

Reason 2. Nearby colors are causing the same gradient color to appear different 

In some cases, gradient colors that are the same can appear to be different due the visual 

effect of nearby colors. 

For example, a medium gradient color will appear lighter when displayed next to a dark 

shade, and darker when displayed next to the light shade. 

Color Scale 

When you select the Color scale option in financial reports, the system automatically applies 

gradients of a color to values. By default, values are highlighted using a single color of your 

choice, with the highest value receiving the darkest shade. 

You can also choose to use a different color for values below a threshold (such as 0 or another 

number, the average, or the median). Values below the threshold are highlighted using the 

selected color, with the lowest value receiving the darkest shade. 

The following example shows two-color scale, where red is used for values below 10,000. 

To apply a color scale: 

1. 
In the Display in report output section, select the Color scale option. 

2. 
Select the color gradient to use. 

3. 
To highlight values that fall below a threshold, select the Use different color for values 

below threshold check box.  

4. 
Select the desired highlight color to apply to values that are below the threshold. 

---


<!-- Page 175 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

• 
Select Custom value to set a custom value. 

• 
Select Average to apply the color to values that fall below the average. 

• 
Select Median to apply the color to values that fall below the median value.  

5. 
Save the report.  

How Color Scale Applies to Reports with Multiple Groupings 

Color scale is computed separately for each top-level account group (such as Expenses). For 

reports that show more than one top-level group (for example, both Revenue and 

Expenses), the color scale for each top-level group is computed separately. This ensures that 

amounts are compared for similar data. 

Within each top-level group, color scale is computed by looking at the range of values 

across all of the lowest-level subgroups.  

Total amounts for subgroups are not included, with the exception of subgroups collapsed to 

show a summary amount.

Trend Indicators 

For any column type that shows a period difference or variance, you can select a trend indicator 
(arrow or dot) and indicate whether an increase is green (good), red (bad), or black. 

If You Import to Excel 

When exported to Excel, columns that contain trend indicators cannot be used in formulas. 

Additionally, because of the way that Excel handles trend indicators, the column containing the 
trend indicators doesn’t display the commas that are used to separate thousands in the number. 
For example, $11,260.00 appears as $11260.00. This appears only in the column with the trend 
indicator. 

Trend Indicator: Period Variance or Difference 

Trend indicators can be used to highlight changes in values, either by amount or percentage, 

from one period to another. For example, you might want to set up a report that shows the 

percentage change in profits for the same month from one year to the next. 

---

Add your Actual columns. The rightmost Actual column should be the prior period that you

2. 
To the right, add a column and set it to either Period variance or Period difference. Select 

the time period that you want to show trending. 

For example: 

Column type: Period variance

just income. Black is a good choice when you have a mix of data.

Troubleshooting Trend Indicators 

• 
Trend Indicator Does Not Appear as an Option 

The Trend indicator option appears only for columns that show differences or variances 

compared to a budget or prior period.  

• 
Can’t Apply Formula to a Column in Excel 

Columns that display a trend indicator cannot be used in an Excel formula. 

Sparklines 

Select Sparkline as your visual indicator to turn a column of numbers into line charts that show 

the change in value over time. With sparklines, rows in the column are displayed as line charts, 

instead of numbers. Each line chart shows the change in value over time. 

Each line chart has a separate y-axis scale based on the minimum and maximum values over the 
expanded time period. Excel output of sparklines requires Excel 2010 or later. For PDF and CSV 
output formats (which don’t support visual indicators), sparkline columns are converted to 
amounts.  

To display a column as sparklines: 

1. 
For the visual indicator, select Sparkline. 

If you do not see sparkline as an option, it may be because sparklines display the variation 
in data expanded over time, and sparkline isn’t available for columns that have been 
expanded by a dimension other than time. To verify the column settings, scroll to the 

Expand by option for the column. 

2. 
Optionally, select the time period to expand by. 

---


<!-- Page 180 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

A default time period is preselected for you. 

3. 
For some reporting periods, you can change the time period (for example, to chart the 

current year by month instead of quarter). 

Selecting Sparkline as your visual indicator automatically sets the “Expand by” option for 
the column to expand by time periods. 

Troubleshooting Sparklines 

• 
Sparkline is not an option 

Because sparklines display the variation in data expanded over time, sparkline isn’t available 

for columns that have been expanded by a dimension other than time. To verify the column 

settings, scroll to the Expand by option for the column. 

• 
How sparkline columns appear in Excel, PDF, or CSV output 

Sparklines appear only when the report is: 

• 
Viewed in Accounting, either in HTML format or as part of a dashboard. 

• 
Output to Excel and opened with Excel 2010 or later. 

Because visual indicators aren’t supported in PDF or CSV output, rows in a sparkline column 

are converted to amounts for the selected reporting period (not expanded by quarter, 

month, or other time period). 

• 
Do all rows in a column use the same scale for the sparkline? 

No. Each sparkline takes up the same amount of space in the report, but the Y-axis for each 

chart has a different minimum and maximum value, based on the minimum and maximum 

values for data points within the reporting period. For example, suppose that the sparkline 

for a row shows actual amounts expanded by quarter, with values of 1200, 7000, 450, and 

100. In this case the Y-axis for the chart extends from 100 (the minimum) to 7000 (the 

maximum).

Other Column Options 

Amount Type 

Every account group has a default method of calculating amounts on reports. For example, 

account groups that contain income or expense accounts are typically calculated “For the period” 

so that reports show the income or expense incurred during that reporting period. 

You can stick with the default amount type, or you can override this calculation method for a 

column in your report. If you’ve already set up an amount type for the rows in your report, the 

Apply rows tab settings option uses the amount type that you selected on the Rows tab. 

Show As 

Select a Show as option to change how a value is displayed. For example, you can display an 

Actual or Budget value as-is, using the Number option. You can also display it as an average over 

time. Additional options are available for computations. 

The options that you see in the drop-down list vary depending on the column type and other 

factors. 

• 
Number: Shows the value as a number. For example, 10,000. 

By default, a currency symbol isn’t displayed, except on totals and subtotal rows. However, 

you can use the Rows and totals options in the Format tab to show or hide currency 

symbols for particular rows. 

• 
Daily average, Weekly average, Monthly average, Quarterly average: For actual or budget 

amounts, displays the amount as an average for an amount of time. For example, if your 

reporting period is the current month, you can display the amount as a daily or weekly 

average. 

• 
Annualize by days, Annualize by months: Takes the amounts for the current year-to-date 

and extrapolates the period to an entire year. This allows you to see, for instance, what your 

estimated expenses would be for the year based on what you’ve spent so far. 

These appear only for columns where the reporting period is Current Year to Date. 

1. 
Set up the column to show amounts for the current year-to-date. 

---


<!-- Page 182 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

• 
Reporting period: Current year-to-date. 

• 
Column type: Typically, an actual column. 

2. 
In the Show as drop-down list, select the Annualize option. 

When you run the report, the system displays the amount as an estimated amount for 

the entire year. 

To annualize by months, the system takes the amount of this column, divides that 

amount by the number of months so far, and then multiplies the result by 12. 

This is a list of options for computed values: 

• 
Number: Shows the value as a number. For example, 10,000. By default, a currency symbol 

isn’t displayed, except on totals and subtotal rows. However, you can use the Rows and 

totals options in the Format tab to show or hide currency symbols for particular rows. 

• 
Amount with currency: Displays amounts with a currency symbol. In this case, the currency 

symbol is displayed for the entire column, even if the Rows and totals option in the Format 

tab is set to hide currency symbols for particular rows. 

• 
Ratio with decimals, Ratio without decimals: Displays the computed value as a ratio 

relative to 1, with or without decimals. Most often used when one value is divided by 

another value. For example, dividing 100 by 400 would result in a 1:4 ratio, which is 

displayed as 4. 

• 
Percent: Applies only to columns of type Computation on actual and Computation on 

budget. For computations that result from division, the result is converted to a percentage 

and displayed with a percent sign. For example, .25 is displayed as 25%. 

• 
Percentage - convert to %: Applies only to columns of type Summary on columns. 

Commonly used for computations that divide two columns, this option converts the result 

of the calculation to a percentage—for example, turning .25 into 25%. 

• 
Percentage - append % sign: Appends a percentage sign, without multiplying by 100 to 

convert to a percentage. For example, .25 is displayed as .25%. Although less commonly 

used, this option is available for columns of type Summary on columns and is the default 

option for period and budget variance columns (which are by definition already 

percentages).

Precision 

The default precision is two decimal places. However, you can override this setting to customize 

the number of decimal places, if the column is used in a calculation that is displayed as 

percentages or ratios that can be rounded. 

If this feature is available, select the column to set the precision digits and choose the level of 

precision from the drop-down list. If precision isn’t valid for the column selections, the selection 

drop-down list isn’t available. 

Reporting Book (GAAP, Tax, or User-Defined) 

You can create other reporting books for entering transactions that are outside of your actual 

books. These might include GAAP adjustments, tax adjustments, or other types of transactions 

that you track in user-defined books. 

By default, amounts from all books are combined together. For example, if you include your GAAP 

book with your Accrual book, the report will show Accrual amounts with the GAAP adjustments 

applied. However, you can choose to exclude the main reporting book to show only the 

adjustments.  

The Reporting book options appear only if you’ve enabled other reporting books in the General 
Ledger, such as GAAP or tax books or user-defined books.

### Computations Tab
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 185*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

Computations Tab 


> **Navigation Path:** `Reports > Reports Center > Financial Reporting > Financial Reports > Edit > 
Computations`



> **Navigation Path:** `General Ledger > All > Reports > Financial Statements > Financial Reports > Edit > 
Computations`


The Computations tab lets you define calculations that you plan to use on the Columns tab of 

your financial report. You can add up to 20 calculations. 

In most cases, computations involve accounts or account groups. This topic shows how to 

calculate expenses as a percentage of total expenses by creating a computation that divides the 

amount in rows by the Expenses account group. 

Besides using the Computations tab, there are other ways to add computations to financial 

reports. 

• 
You can add computations to rows. To add a computation to a summary column, see 

Adding computations to rows (on page 153). 

• 
The Computations tab appears only if you selected Accounts as your report structure rather 

than segments or dimensions. However, all types of financial reports provide the option to 

add a summary column that computes a value from other columns, such as computing the 

average across a set of columns. 

How Computations Work 

To understand how computations work, consider a case in which you want to create an expense 

report that calculates your expenses as a percentage of total expenses. 

Column 3 is a computed column of the actual expenses (entries in column 2) divided by total 

expenses (total of column 2) to show percentages. 

To calculate this for your report, you would define a computation on the Computations tab, and 

then use it in the Columns tab. 

1. 
On the Computations tab, you define a computation that divides your expense account 

groups by your total expenses (represented by the account group called Expenses).

### Advanced Computations
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 188*

Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

Advanced Computations 

Adding Columns for Complex Computations 

One blank computation column is created for you by default, but you can add more columns for 

additional computations. In some cases, you may need more than one computation to get the 

calculation that you need. A common technique for this is to create more than one “Compute on 

actual” column for your report, and to hide any columns that are performing interim calculations. 

Hiding Columns Used Only for Computations 

The option to hide a column appears on the Columns tab. 

• 
Scroll to the bottom of the column that you want to hide, and then select the Hide Column 

check box. 

Computations on Expanded Columns 

You can’t apply a computation to a column that is expanded by time or segment and have the 

computation apply to the entire set of expanded columns. However, there are other ways to 

handle computations to get the calculation you need.

Defining a Computation 

Use the Create computation page to define a computation that you plan to use on the Columns 

tab of your financial report. Learn more about how computations work. 

Defining a Computation 

A computation consists of three parts (account group, operation, and value) and is meant to be 

read from left to right. The following example illustrates the meaning of a computation that uses 

division to calculate amounts as a percentage of total expenses. 

a) This indicates whether the computation applies to the entire column or to a specific account 

group. 

---


<!-- Page 190 -->
Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc.

b) This is the selected operator that the system uses in the computation. 

c) This is the object of the operation. 

In this example, the computation applies to all columns in the report. It divides each account 

group amount by the total for the account group called Expenses. 

When to Create a Calculation for a Specific Group 

You can apply a computation to the entire column or to a specific account group. The 

Computations tab displays your account groups along the left side to give you the option of 

applying different calculations to the different account groups. 

Suppose that you were create an Income & Expense report. You might decide that Computation 1 

should apply a different calculation to income than to expenses. 

• 
For income account groups, you might divide income by headcount. 

• 
For expense account groups, you might divide expenses by total expenses to get the 

percentage spent on each type of expense. 

To define a computation: 

1. 
Verify the account group to which you are applying the computation. 

• 
To apply a calculation to all account groups in the report, open the Computation 

drop-down list at the top of the computation, and then select Set computations. 

• 
To apply a calculation to a specific account group, locate the account group in the 

Computations on groups column, and then click the Computation column. 

---


<!-- Page 191 -->
Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports 

© 2026 RealPage, Inc. 

The Create computation box opens. 

2. 
In the Create computation box, select the operation that you want to perform. You can 

choose from several predefined operations, such as Add, Subtract, Subtract from, Multiply, 

Divide, and Divide into. 

To understand what each operation does, keep in mind that the system applies the 

computation to the amounts in an actual or budget column that you select on the Columns 

tab. 

• 
Add: Takes the actual or budget amount and adds the value that you specify in the 

next step. 

• 
Subtract: Takes an actual or budget amount and subtracts the value that you specify in 

the next step. 

• 
Subtract from: Takes the value that you specify in the next step and subtracts the 

actual or budget amount. 

• 
Multiply: Takes an actual or budget amount and multiplies it by the value that you 

specify in the next step. 

• 
Divide: Takes an actual or budget amount and divides it by the value that you specify 

in the next step. 

• 
Divide into: Takes the value that you specify in the next step and divides it by the 

actual or budget amount. 

• 
Hide report cell: Hides amounts for the selected account group. For example, you 

might want to hide salary amounts or other sensitive information from a report. 

This option applies only to account groups that have not been expanded by dimension. 

3. 
Use the Variable type and Variable value options to determine where the report should get 

the value to be used in the computation. 

If you select an account group or account, the value is determined dynamically based on the 

value for the account group or account for the reporting period selected on the Columns 

tab. 

• 
Account group: Sets the value to the total for an account group of your choice. 

• 
Account: Sets the value to the amount for an account of your choice. 

• 
Constant: Sets the value to a number that you specify, such as 100. 

For complex calculations (on page 188) (such as x plus y, divided by z), you can use more 
than one computation in combination with hidden columns.

•

You can also enable the Prompt option to allow users to select report filters at runtime. In

Setting the Repo;rting Period and Reporting Book 

Specifying the As of Date 

Reporting periods are always relative to the As of date for the report. In most cases, you’ll want to 

leave the date blank and select the Prompt check box so that you’ll be prompted for the date 

when you run the report. 

To help you identify the As of date in your report output, you can dynamically include the “As of 
date” in your report header or footer. 

Type “p” in a date field to automatically insert the last day of the prior month. See Specifying 

Dates in Getting Started for a full list of shortcut keys related to entering dates.  

If you enabled the “p” in the As of Date field of the Filters section on the Schedule Financial 

Report page, select the Run as of the last day of the prior month check box to schedule reports 

and reports groups to run at that time. 

Selecting a Reporting Book 

Use the Reporting book filter to select the main reporting book to be used for the report. This 

option appears only if you have more than one way of reporting on your actual books. 

• 
If you opted for dual method reporting in the General Ledger, decide whether you want to 

create an Accrual or Cash report. 

• 
If you set up GAAP, Tax, or User-defined reporting books, then you can include these books 

on a column-by-column basis. Learn more about reporting on other books.

Filtering by Location, Department, or Other Dimension 

In addition to the default dimensions for departments and locations, your company may use 

other dimensions to track transactions. These dimensions let you filter reports in multiple ways; 

for instance, by showing data from only certain locations or customers. 

If you apply more than one filter, then the report will contain the subset of data that meets all of 

the filter criteria. For example, if you choose “Sales” as the department and “Arizona” as the 

location, then the report will include data only for the Sales department at the Arizona location. 

Filter for a Specific Dimension Member 

For any dimension that you’ve enabled, you can select an individual member to filter by. For 

example, you might filter a report for a specific location, department, or customer. 

To filter for a specific location, department, or other dimension member: 

1. 
Locate the dimension filter and select the option for Specific dimension/group. 

For example, to filter for a location, go to the Location drop-down list and choose the 

Specific location/group option. 

2. 
In the drop-down list that appears, select the dimension member by which you want to 

filter. 

• 
Using location as an example, choose the name of the location by which you want to 

filter. 

• 
The drop-down lists contain all available dimension groups, followed by individual 

dimension members, sorted alphabetically by ID. 

3. 
If you want the option to change the filter selection when you run the report, select the 

Prompt check box. 

4. 
When you expand rows or columns by department or location, the report automatically 

combines the data together in a single report. To generate a separate report for each 

department or location, select the Run as individual reports check box. 

When the report is generated as PDF, each individual report starts on a new page. In HTML 
and Excel, each department or location appears in a separate section. 

5. 
To exclude inactive dimensions from reports that meet certain criteria, select the Hide 

Inactive check box. For example, you prevent departments or locations you are no longer 

using from appearing in columns or rows. 

6. 
If you want to generate the report to display only the transactions not associated with any 

dimension, select the Only blank check box. 

If you want a separate report for each department or location, learn more about creating 

individual reports. 

---


<!-- Page 194 -->

Filter for Two or More Dimension Members Using Groups 

Use dimension groups if you want to filter for two or more dimensions. A dimension group is a 

name for particular set of members in a dimension, or a set of members that meet certain criteria. 

For example, you might create groups for: 

• 
A set of locations (such as your US locations) 

• 
Group by a certain type (such as Vendor type or Customer type) 

• 
Specific customers, customers located in a particular state, or even customers with the 

greatest open balance 

To filter for a dimension group or type: 

1. 
Locate the Define dimension filters in the list of dimensions, and then select the option for 

Specific dimension/group. 

For example, to filter by location, go to the Location drop-down list and choose Specific 

location/group. 

2. 
In the drop-down list that appears, select a dimension group or type, or click Add to create 

a new group on the fly. 

• 
If you’ve defined dimension groups (such as location groups or customer groups), 

these groups will appear first, before any specific dimension members. 

• 
To create a new group, click Add at the top of the drop-down list. 

3. 
If you want the option to change the filter selection when you run the report, select the 

Prompt check box. 

4. 
If you want to generate the report to display only the transactions not associated with any 

dimension, select the Only blank check box. 

Dimension Type 

Many dimensions can be tagged to types and groups. Customer types and vendor types can also 

have parent types for filtering. 

Categorize records according to type for filtering, sorting, and grouping opportunities. These 

types can take advantage of an additional layer of grouping by assigning a dimension type. If you 

assign a dimension type within your types, you can also get a native roll-up of any types assigned 

the dimension type during reporting. 

For example, if you set up the vendor types as Contractor and Subcontractor and make 

Contractor the parent type of Subcontractor—and then you filter financial reports using the 

Contractor vendor type—all vendors assigned to Contractor and Subcontractor will be included in 

the report. 

To filter for a dimension type:

1. 
In the Dimension type drop-down list, select the dimension type you want to filter. 

2. 
In the Values drop-down list, select the value for the dimension type. 

3. 
If you are adding a filter, select the applicable Filter condition in the drop-down list, and 

then click the Add filter link. 

4.

5.

Prompting for Filters at Runtime 

You can prompt users for selected filters when you run the report. 

While it’s typical to prompt users for the “As of date” for a report, it’s also common to prompt for 

the location, department, or other criteria. For example, instead of creating a balance sheet report 

that is always filtered for a particular location, you can use the Prompt option to enable users to 

choose a location or location group. 

How the Prompt Option Works 

If you select the Prompt check box for a segment, the system asks for this information when you 

run the report. The user who runs the report chooses the account group or segment structure to 

filter by. 

By choosing to prompt at runtime, you can set up one report and use it multiple ways, such as 

setting up a balance sheet report and then running it for different locations on the fly. 

If you select specific segment filters and also select the Prompt check box, then the system 

automatically fills in the report prompt with your selections. However, you can override the filters. 

Example: Prompting for G/L Account Groups or Reporting Periods 

You can dynamically run financial reports on a G/L account group other than what the report was 

originally set up for (account groups are defined (on page 144) on the Rows tab of the Financial 

report writer). To do this, enable the Prompt for G/L account groups option in the financial 

report. This allows you to choose an alternate G/L account group when you run the report rather 

than duplicating a report and changing the account group(s). 

Additionally, you can enable the Prompt for reporting periods check box to dynamically run 

financial reports for a reporting period, column heading, and expand by. Columns for Actual, 

Budget, Remaining budget, Open commitments, and Pending commitments appear in the 

prompt.

does not apply to financial reports that are available in Site Experience. 

When you Run, Schedule, or Process & store the report, you can select one or more account 

groups or reporting periods. The order in which you select the account groups or reporting 

periods will be the order in which they appear in the report. Additionally, you can run individual 

reports for each department or location.

#### Using Dimension Groups to Specify Order in Rows and Columns
*Source: `RP Accounting Reports User Guide.pdf`, Page 197*

Book II: Using RealPage Accounting Reports

Using Dimension Groups to Specify Order in Rows and Columns 

In financial reports, you can expand rows or columns by dimension. For example, you can expand 

an actual column into several columns by location, department, or other dimension. 

To control the order of members in rows or columns: 

Workflow 

1. 
Create a dimension group that contains the desired members. 

In the dimension group, order the members as you want them to be listed in reports. 

2. 
Filter the report by the dimension group. 

How Location and Department Filters Work 

When you make selections for Department and Location, the following rules apply: 

• 
The calculations are based on the combination of the specified department and location. 

For example, if you chose the Manufacturing department and the California location, the 

calculations are based on numbers only for Manufacturing departments that are also 

located in California. 

• 
All children of parent departments and locations are included in the calculations. 

• 
If you created a department hierarchy using a parent/child relationship, you can report on 

the parent department or the individual child department by selecting the department 

name from the drop-down list. If you choose a parent department, the system retrieves all 

the information from the child departments assigned to that parent and displays the 

information with that of the parent as a rolled-up total. 

• 
If you are a multi-entity shared user of the ownership financials and distribution feature, you 

can select a location only if the owner you select in the Report on owner field has some 

percentage ownership in the entity under which the location falls.
